addressed_problems.content: In reinforcement learning, the benefit of winning-ticket initializations (i.e., subnetworks pruned via iterative magnitude pruning and late rewinding) over random initializations varies substantially across environments: some Atari games (e.g., Assault, Seaquest, Berzerk) show clear performance gains, while others (e.g., Breakout, Centipede, Krull) show little or no benefit, and one game (Kangaroo) even sees learning enabled where none was possible. The underlying cause of this heterogeneity—whether it arises from differences in effective over-parameterization, optimization landscape, sensitivity to the shared hyperparameter configuration, or other factors—remains unresolved. Resolving this question is important for understanding when and why lottery-ticket phenomena occur in RL and for developing pruning strategies that reliably produce winning tickets across diverse environments.

The precise dependence of winning-ticket discovery on pruning schedules (e.g., iterative vs. one-shot), rewinding epoch choice, and other optimizer/hyperparameter settings (e.g., learning rate, optimizer type, batch size) has not been fully characterized across the different architectures and domains studied. Although the paper uses an iterative pruning rate of 0.2 and late rewinding to after one epoch for RL, the optimal values of these parameters for different architectures (e.g., LSTMs, Transformers, convolutional networks) and tasks (language modeling, translation, control, Atari) are not established. A systematic study is needed to determine how these factors interact with the lottery ticket phenomenon and to provide guidelines for efficient ticket search.

The study demonstrates that a Transformer Big model can be trained from a pruned initialization to within 99% of the unpruned BLEU score at 67% sparsity (28.9 vs. 29.2 BLEU), but realizing the computational and memory benefits of such sparsity in practice requires efficient sparse-matrix multiplication libraries and inference runtimes. Such systems are outside the scope of this work, and their development remains an open engineering challenge. Without them, the practical gains from lottery tickets in large-scale NLP models cannot be fully realized.

The experiments reveal high run-to-run variance in the performance of winning tickets in some RL settings, necessitating multiple pruning seeds to obtain reliable results. Understanding the sources of this variance—whether from random seeds, initialization, environment stochasticity, or the pruning process itself—and developing methods to reduce it remains an open problem. Lower variance would improve the reliability of ticket evaluation and facilitate the practical use of lottery tickets in RL.

It remains open whether winning ticket masks and initializations discovered in one RL environment or under one random seed generalize to related tasks or different seeds. The current work does not evaluate the transferability of tickets across environments or seeds, and understanding this property could lead to reusable sparse subnetworks that accelerate learning across multiple RL tasks.

The work exclusively uses unstructured magnitude-based pruning to find winning tickets. Whether structured pruning methods (e.g., filter or channel pruning) or alternative ranking criteria (e.g., gradient-based, variational) could yield better or more transferable winning tickets in NLP and RL is not addressed. Investigating these alternatives could reveal more efficient or practical pruning strategies that maintain the lottery ticket phenomenon while being better suited to hardware acceleration.

The lottery ticket phenomenon has been demonstrated in supervised image classification, NLP (LSTMs and Transformers), and RL (classic control and Atari), but it remains unclear whether it extends uniformly to other large-scale tasks (e.g., video understanding, speech recognition), training regimes (e.g., meta-learning, self-supervised learning), or architectures not evaluated here (e.g., graph neural networks, memory-augmented networks). Establishing the generality of the lottery ticket hypothesis is important for understanding its underlying mechanisms and for guiding its application to a broader range of deep learning problems.

The lottery ticket hypothesis—i.e., that over-parameterized deep neural networks (DNNs) often contain small, sparse sub-networks whose initializations enable training in isolation to match or exceed the performance of parameter-matched random sub-networks—has been studied mainly for supervised image classification with feed-forward convolutional networks. Prior work established the phenomenon for small image tasks and identified important training heuristics (e.g., iterative magnitude pruning, learning-rate warmup, late rewinding) but also showed conflicting results for larger models and other architectures: large learning rates and different optimization schedules can destroy the effect, and some studies reported that random sub-networks can match "winning tickets" in ResNets and Transformers. At the same time, modern applications place emphasis on architectures and learning regimes very different from small supervised image tasks—recurrent gated models (LSTMs) used for language modeling, multi-layer Transformer encoders/decoders used for large-scale machine translation, and reinforcement learning (RL) agents that train from non-stationary, reward-driven data streams. Because these architectures (gating, recurrence, self-attention) and learning regimes (reward-driven, non-stationary data distributions, asynchronous/off-policy optimization) change the optimization dynamics and parameter usage of networks, it remained unresolved whether (a) winning-ticket initializations exist in NLP and RL at realistic scales, (b) whether the pruning/resetting procedures found useful in prior image work (iterative pruning, late rewinding) are necessary or sufficient in these domains, and (c) whether identifying such sparse, trainable initializations could produce practically deployable, smaller models without large performance loss. These gaps prevent principled conclusions about the generality of the lottery ticket phenomenon, leave unanswered which parts of modern architectures (e.g., embeddings vs. Transformer layers) are critically dependent on initialization, and impede understanding of when and how sparse initializations can reduce model size or enable learning in regimes (e.g., certain Atari games) where training is unstable.

nodes.content: Language modeling with recurrent LSTM architectures is a representative NLP task where gating and recurrent dynamics alter optimization trajectories compared to feed-forward convolutional models. Prior lottery-ticket studies focused on supervised image tasks and did not establish whether the same initialization-based explanation for over-parameterization holds when recurrence and gating interact with truncated BPTT, embedding layers, and common NLP optimizers. Earlier pruning studies often used one-shot pruning or did not apply late rewinding; those choices can mask whether a sub-network's initialization, rather than the pruning procedure or optimization artifacts, is responsible for trainability. Without evidence for LSTMs, it was unclear whether sparse, trainable initializations could be found for recurrent NLP models or whether recurrence/gates would preclude lottery-ticket phenomena, preventing both theoretical generalization and practical parameter reduction for language models.

Transformer architectures used in large-scale machine translation combine large embedding matrices with deep stacked self-attention and feed-forward layers; prior work reported contradictory evidence about whether lottery tickets exist in Transformers. Some prior negative results used one-shot pruning and omitted late rewinding, leaving open whether the negative outcome was due to the pruning/resetting method rather than an architectural limitation of Transformers. Practitioners need to know which parameter subsets (embeddings vs. Transformer layers) can be sparsified without loss and whether careful pruning/resetting recovers trainability for pruned Transformer layers. Without such knowledge, one cannot safely reduce model size for deployment or fully understand how initialization interacts with self-attention and embedding parameterization.

Transformer Big models are state-of-the-art for many sequence-to-sequence tasks but are often too large for cost-effective training and deployment. Prior lottery-ticket investigations left unresolved whether extreme sparsification (retaining only a fraction of parameters) is compatible with high-end Transformer performance, especially at large scale where training dynamics, optimizer settings, and initialization sensitivity differ from small-image benchmarks. If winning-ticket initializations could be found that permit training much smaller Transformers from scratch to near-original performance, it would enable substantial computational and deployment gains. However, without empirical proof at Big-model scale, claims about practical compressibility and the generality of the lottery-ticket effect remained speculative.

Reinforcement learning optimizes policies from non-stationary, reward-driven data distributions, which substantially alter gradient statistics and effective sample distributions compared to supervised learning. It was unknown whether winning-ticket initializations that benefit supervised image and NLP training also exist for RL, where exploration, credit assignment, and asynchronous/off-policy updates can interact with sparsity and initialization in complex ways. Without evidence in simple RL control tasks, the community lacked confidence that sparse trainable initializations could be found for RL agents or that sparse initialization strategies could improve learning stability or sample efficiency in policy optimization.

Pixel-based RL (Atari) couples convolutional feature extraction to policy/value heads and experiences complex, game-specific sample distributions and reward structures. Prior lottery-ticket work focused on static supervised datasets and could not reveal whether the phenomenon survives the non-stationarity and exploration-exploitation challenges of pixel-control RL. Moreover, practical RL research often uses common hyperparameters across many environments, leaving open whether a single pruning/initialization strategy would produce uniformly compressible agents. Without empirical characterization across multiple games, researchers and practitioners cannot predict whether sparsification will preserve performance, or whether some games are effectively over-parameterized while others require denser networks or specialized pruning schemes.

The original lottery ticket paradigm reset pruned weights to their initial ($j=0$) values; subsequent work found that late rewinding (resetting to early-training weights) substantially helps large-scale networks. It remained unclear which pruning/resetting choices are necessary and sufficient across architectures and learning regimes—especially given earlier negative reports for Transformers and ResNets that did not use iterative pruning or late rewinding. Practitioners need to know whether iterative pruning and/or late rewinding are required to find trainable sparse initializations in NLP and RL, and which of these modifications is more critical, because such choices affect the feasibility of discovering winning tickets at scale and the computational cost of iterative pruning experiments.

A two-layer long short-term memory (LSTM) language model with hidden state size 650, word-embedding size 650, trained on the Wikitext-2 language modeling dataset with truncated backpropagation through time of length 50, batch size 30, optimized by Adam with learning rate 10^{-3} and β1=0.9, β2=0.999, ε=10^{-3}, and trained for 10 epochs, was subjected to global iterative magnitude pruning (global magnitude pruning pools all scalar weight and bias magnitudes across layers and removes the lowest-magnitude parameters) using an iterative pruning rate p = 0.2 and late rewinding of the surviving weights to their values after the first epoch of training; the sparse sub-networks (the "winning tickets") obtained by this procedure, when reinitialized to those rewound weights and retrained under the same optimizer and training regimen, achieve lower test-set log perplexity than parameter-matched randomly initialized sparse networks (random tickets obtained by drawing new random initial weights and applying the same sparsity mask) across every tested global pruning fraction, and retain high performance even when up to 90% of the parameters are removed (at these extreme pruning levels the winning-ticket retrainings show little to no increase in test-set log perplexity relative to the unpruned model, whereas the parameter-matched random-ticket retrainings degrade substantially).

metadata.narrative: The LSTM conclusion is credibly supported by within-experiment ablations (H1) that isolate iterative pruning and rewinding and by the clear curves in Fig. 1 showing winning tickets beat random tickets across pruning levels. The dominant residual risk is generalization: P1 flags that the finding is based on a single dataset and a single fixed architecture/hyperparameter choice, so while the conclusion that winning tickets exist for this two-layer LSTM configuration is well supported (H1 underwrites the mechanism and comparative advantage), the claim's scope should be read as applying to the reported LSTM protocol rather than to all LSTMs. P6 (comparative fairness of random baselines) is a secondary risk: if random-ticket training were re-tuned per mask the gap might shrink, but the ablation evidence still gives substantial credit that initialization matters under the paper's training recipe.

nodes.title: Two-layer LSTM winning tickets on Wikitext-2 outperform random tickets across pruning levels

nodes.content: Transformer models trained on the WMT'14 English→German machine translation task, evaluated by case-sensitive tokenized BLEU computed with multi-bleu.pl on Newstest2014, were pruned using global iterative magnitude pruning (iterative pruning rate p = 0.2) and evaluated with late rewinding of surviving weights to an early-trained checkpoint (for the Transformer experiments the surviving weights were in experiments compared to the parameters after 1000 updates); the resulting sparse sub-networks (winning-ticket initializations), when reinitialized to those rewound weights and retrained under the same training recipe and checkpoint-averaging procedure, outperform parameter-matched randomly initialized sparse networks (random tickets) across pruning fractions, and two empirical patterns were observed: (a) for the Transformer Base model whose unpruned baseline BLEU on Newstest2014 is 27.6, winning-ticket retrainings preserve BLEU substantially better than parameter-matched random-ticket retrainings across pruning fractions; and (b) in experiments that pruned only the Transformer layer weights (the attention and feed-forward fully connected layer matrices and biases) while leaving the embedding matrices unpruned, random-ticket performance degraded rapidly with pruning whereas winning-ticket performance remained robust and decreased roughly linearly in BLEU as the fraction of Transformer-layer weights removed increased, indicating that the large embedding matrices respond differently to pruning than Transformer-layer weights and that winning tickets primarily protect performance of the Transformer layers under pruning.

metadata.narrative: The Transformer-base conclusion is strengthened by a targeted pruning ablation that separates transformer-layer-only pruning from full global pruning (H2), and by iterative-pruning ablations that mirror the LSTM findings (H6). The primary weak point is P2: because pruning is global, the apparent embedding vs. transformer-layer difference could be an artifact of parameter-mass and ranking rather than an intrinsic sensitivity; this risk does not invalidate the empirical observation under the paper's protocol, but it narrows the interpretation (the finding is robust for the evaluated pruning procedure, but attribution to embeddings as a fundamentally different class requires further isolation). Comparative-fairness concerns about the random baseline (P6) also modestly temper the strength but do not overturn the observed transformer-layer robustness reported with the winning-ticket initialization.

nodes.title: Transformer winning tickets on WMT'14 En→De; embeddings and layer pruning differ

nodes.content: A Transformer Big model of approximately 210 million parameters trained on WMT'14 English→German that the paper reports with an unpruned BLEU of 29.2 was pruned by global iterative magnitude pruning with late rewinding to produce a model retaining 33% of parameters (67% sparsity); when the pruned sub-network was reinitialized to the winning-ticket rewound weights and retrained under the same Transformer training recipe (including checkpoint averaging), it achieved BLEU = 28.9 on Newstest2014, which the paper reports as approximately 99% of the unpruned-model BLEU (28.9 BLEU at 67% pruned versus 29.2 BLEU unpruned).

metadata.narrative: The Transformer Big result is an important computational highlight (H3) demonstrating the phenomenon at realistic scale, which materially raises the paper's practical relevance. However, P3 is the dominant risk: the reported 0.3 BLEU gap is small and presented without run-level variance or multiple independent repeats, so the numerical claim of retaining "~99% BLEU" is fragile to training noise and may not generalize robustly across seeds. In short, the qualitative claim that large Transformers admit winning-ticket retraining is supported, but the quantitative claim of reliably achieving 99% BLEU at 67% sparsity requires stronger statistical backing (additional runs / confidence intervals) to be fully secured.

nodes.title: Transformer Big pruned to 67% sparsity attains BLEU 28.9 (~99%)

nodes.content: In three discrete-action classic control OpenAI Gym environments—CartPole-v0, Acrobot-v1, and LunarLander-v2—each trained with the A2C (advantage actor-critic) optimizer and simple fully-connected multi-layer perceptron (MLP) policies whose layer sizes are MLP(128-128-128-out) for CartPole-v0 and MLP(256-256-256-out) for Acrobot-v1 and LunarLander-v2 (network specifications as given in Table A1), applying global iterative magnitude pruning with iterative pruning rate p = 0.2 and late rewinding of surviving weights to their values after a small initial training period produced sparse sub-networks (winning tickets) that, when reinitialized to those rewound weights and retrained under the same A2C training recipe, yielded higher averaged episodic reward over the final evaluation episodes than parameter-matched randomly initialized sparse networks (random tickets obtained by drawing new random initial weights and applying the same sparsity mask) across the tested global pruning levels; this winning-ticket advantage was observed consistently across three independent iterative-pruning runs per game (results reported as mean ± standard deviation across the three runs).

metadata.narrative: The classic-control RL conclusion is supported by consistent mean±std curves across three pruning runs per game (H4), which provides direct evidence that winning tickets can outperform random tickets in simple RL control settings. The principal weak point is statistical/generalization (P4): the small number of seeds and limited game set mean the result is credible for the tested configurations but not yet a general theorem about RL; nonetheless, because H4 documents repeated runs and clear, consistent trends, the conclusion that winning tickets exist in these classic-control tasks is reasonably well underwritten, with the caveat that broader RL generalization remains uncertain.

nodes.title: Winning tickets in classic-control A2C MLPs outperform random tickets

nodes.content: For nine Atari games trained with a common convolutional policy network (Conv(5,64,1,2)-MaxPool(2)-Conv(5,64,1,2)-MaxPool(2)-Conv(3,64,1,1)-MaxPool(2)-Conv(3,64,1,1)-MaxPool(2)-MLP(1920-512-512-out) as summarized in Table A1) and A2C with importance-factor correction and shared hyperparameters across games, global iterative magnitude pruning with late rewinding produced heterogeneous outcomes across games: some games (Assault, Seaquest, Berzerk, Qbert) showed substantial average reward improvements for winning-ticket initializations relative to parameter-matched random tickets; other games (Breakout, Centipede) were highly sensitive to pruning and performance degraded quickly for both ticket types; at least one game (Krull) exhibited little difference between winning and random tickets even at extreme pruning (interpreted as extreme over-parameterization for that task); and in the game Kangaroo—where the unpruned network trained under the shared hyperparameter settings failed to converge to typical high rewards—the winning-ticket initializations substantially improved learning relative to random tickets, enabling nonzero learning that the unpruned configuration did not achieve.

metadata.narrative: The Atari conclusion correctly emphasizes heterogeneity: the paper's nine-game suite and explicit reporting (H5) substantiate that outcomes are game-dependent and that in some cases (e.g., Kangaroo) winning-ticket initialization enables learning where the unpruned shared-hyperparameter baseline did not. The dominant weaknesses (P4 and P6) are that limited seeds and a single shared set of hyperparameters leave open whether the observed heterogeneity stems from masks/initializations or from hyperparameter mismatch; consequently the conclusion is best read as an empirical catalog of per-game behaviors under the paper's protocol rather than as a universal statement about pixel-control RL.

nodes.title: Atari outcomes are game-dependent; some winning tickets enable learning where unpruned failed

nodes.content: Across the experiments reported for LSTM language modeling on Wikitext-2, Transformer machine translation on WMT'14 English→German, classic-control A2C MLPs, and Atari pixel-control games, using global iterative magnitude pruning (the paper uses an iterative pruning rate p = 0.2 and, for the RL experiments, up to 20 iterative pruning iterations) together with late rewinding of surviving weights to their values after a small number of initial training iterations (the paper uses rewinding to the weights after the first epoch for the LSTM language-modeling experiments and for RL experiments, and for Transformer experiments compares rewinding to the parameters after 1000 updates) yields sparse initializations (winning tickets) that outperform one-shot pruning or resetting to iteration j = 0; ablation experiments reported in the study show that removing iterative pruning substantially degrades sparse-model retraining performance (often causing winning-ticket retrainings to perform no better than parameter-matched random-ticket retrainings at moderate-to-high sparsity), while removing late rewinding causes a smaller but measurable performance loss in some settings, leading the authors to conclude that iterative pruning is the dominant required modification for reliably finding winning tickets in the evaluated NLP and RL settings.

metadata.narrative: The procedural claim that iterative pruning plus late rewinding materially improves winning-ticket discovery is supported by cross-task ablations (H6) that consistently show iterative pruning has the larger effect; this is the paper's strongest methodological contribution. The main caveat (P5) is that the paper fixes the iterative-pruning rate and typically uses a single rewinding epoch (epoch 1) without exhaustive parameter sweeps, so while the conclusion that iterative pruning is essential under the explored hyperparameter choices is well supported, asserting that iterative pruning is the universally dominant modification across all architectures and hyperparameter regimes is somewhat overreaching pending more systematic hyperparameter sensitivity analysis.

nodes.title: Iterative pruning plus late rewinding improves winning-ticket discovery; iterative pruning dominant

nodes.content: The experimental evidence for winning tickets in two-layer LSTMs comes from a single language-modeling dataset (Wikitext-2) and a single LSTM configuration and training recipe: a two-layer LSTM with hidden size 650 and embedding size 650, dropout between RNN layers with probability 0.5, truncated BPTT length 50, batch size 30, optimized with Adam at learning rate 10^{-3} (β1=0.9, β2=0.999, ε=10^{-3}), trained for 10 epochs, using global iterative magnitude pruning with iterative pruning rate p = 0.2 and late rewinding to the weights after the first epoch; therefore the claim that "winning tickets exist for two-layer LSTMs" in the reported experiments is based on this single dataset and this single, fixed training configuration rather than on a systematic sweep across LSTM architectures, datasets, or optimizer settings. Fig. 1

metadata.failure_mode: If the lottery-ticket advantage is specific to the Wikitext-2 dataset or to the exact hyperparameters used (for example, if longer BPTT, a different learning rate, or a larger vocabulary removes the advantage), then the conclusion "winning-ticket initializations exist for two-layer LSTMs" must be narrowed from a claim about LSTMs in general to a claim about this single experimental configuration; specifically, the paper's interpretation that recurrent gating + truncated BPTT generally admits winning tickets would be unsupported and the practical generality (applicability to other LSTM language-modeling setups) would collapse. The intermediate link that fails is the implicit transfer from one empirical configuration to the class of LSTM models; the scope of damage is a narrowing of the conclusion's claimed domain (from "LSTMs" generally to "this LSTM + Wikitext-2 protocol").
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's LSTM result is based on one dataset and one fixed architecture/hyperparameter configuration; the lottery-ticket effect can be sensitive to dataset size, sequence length, optimizer choice, truncation length, learning-rate schedule, or other architectural hyperparameters. Because these factors materially affect optimization and sparsity tolerance in recurrent models, a single-config demonstration is insufficient to establish the claim for "two-layer LSTMs" as a class rather than for that specific experimental instantiation.

nodes.title: LSTM evidence limited to single dataset and fixed training recipe

nodes.content: The observation that embeddings behave differently from Transformer-layer weights under pruning is drawn from experiments that use global magnitude pruning (which pools all scalar weight and bias magnitudes across layers when selecting parameters to remove) and from a controlled comparison between two pruning regimes: (i) pruning all model parameters in the global pool (including large embedding matrices), and (ii) pruning only Transformer layer weights (attention and fully-connected layer weights and biases) while keeping the embedding matrices unpruned; because the conclusion compares these two specific global-pruning-based regimes, the reported difference in embedding versus Transformer-layer sensitivity reflects that experimental setup rather than an analysis that isolates structured or per-layer pruning alternatives. Fig. 2 (right)

metadata.failure_mode: If the embedding-vs-layer disparity arises primarily because global-magnitude pruning prunes many embedding parameters (or preserves them) due to their magnitude distribution rather than because embeddings are intrinsically more/less compressible, then the conclusion that "winning tickets principally protect Transformer-layer performance" is overstated. Mechanistically, the claimed interpretive attribution (that embeddings are a qualitatively different subsystem in terms of initialization-dependence) would be undermined; the safe conclusion would instead be that the observed behavior depends on pruning granularity and ranking method, not necessarily on a fundamental role for embeddings.
metadata.weakness_reason: Global magnitude pruning orders weights across all parameters, so very large parameter blocks (embeddings) disproportionately influence which parameters are pruned at a given global fraction; as a result, differences observed when pruning "only transformer layers" versus "all weights" can reflect this unequal parameter mass and the particular global-magnitude ranking procedure rather than an intrinsic difference in the sensitivity of embeddings versus transformer layers. The paper does not provide an analysis that isolates whether the observed effect is due to the pruning algorithm's global accounting or to genuine functional sensitivity differences.

nodes.title: Embedding vs Transformer-layer pruning comparison depends on global magnitude pruning

nodes.content: The claim that a pruned Transformer Big model (≈210M parameters) retrained from a winning-ticket initialization achieves BLEU = 28.9 at 67% sparsity versus 29.2 BLEU for the unpruned model is reported as single-point BLEU values in the paper (28.9 vs. 29.2) without accompanying run-to-run variance estimates, multiple independent retraining runs, or statistical tests to assess whether the observed 0.3 BLEU difference is robust to training noise, different random seeds, checkpoint-averaging choices, or evaluation preprocessing. Fig. 3

metadata.failure_mode: If independent repetitions or modest perturbations in training (different random seeds, different checkpoint averaging windows, slight hyperparameter tweaks) produce larger BLEU fluctuations that regularly exceed 0.3 BLEU, then the practical claim that Transformer Big can be pruned to one-third of parameters while retaining ~99% BLEU is not robust: the conclusion would need to be softened to "one reported run achieved 28.9 BLEU at 67% sparsity", and the claim about reliable practical compressibility at that level would be unsupported. The intermediate failure is the mapping from one reported score to a statement of reliable equivalence across training variability.
metadata.weakness_reason: The reported 0.3 BLEU difference is small compared to typical run-to-run variation in large NMT training, and the paper does not provide multiple independent training seeds, confidence intervals, or a significance analysis for the Big-model comparison. Without quantifying variability arising from random initialization, data ordering, checkpoint averaging, or other nondeterministic aspects of large-scale training, it is uncertain whether the pruned model truly achieves "≈99%" of unpruned performance in a robust sense rather than by a fortuitous low-variance run.

nodes.title: Transformer Big BLEU comparison reported as single numbers without run-level variance

nodes.content: The reinforcement-learning results reported for both classic control and Atari experiments summarize performance using means and standard deviations computed from three independent iterative-pruning processes (three pruning runs) per game, and all nine Atari games were trained with a single shared set of RL hyperparameters and A2C configuration rather than with per-game hyperparameter tuning, so the reported Atari results reflect this small number of pruning seeds and the use of shared hyperparameters across diverse games. Fig. 4

metadata.failure_mode: If the winning-ticket advantage in some RL games is highly dependent on random seeds or on the shared hyperparameters (i.e., some seeds/hyperparams yield no advantage or worse performance for winning tickets), then the conclusion that "winning tickets exist in classical RL control tasks and outperform random tickets" would be qualified: it would apply only under the particular seed/hyperparameter ensemble tested rather than as a general RL phenomenon. The intermediate breakdown is that limited-seed statistics and fixed hyperparameters cannot distinguish genuine initialization advantages from stochastic/training-hyperparameter artifacts; the scope of damage is a reduction in the generality and reliability of the RL claims.
metadata.weakness_reason: Three pruning runs provide only a coarse estimate of variability for high-variance RL training; many RL metrics exhibit heavy-tailed or non-Gaussian variability and require larger numbers of seeds to estimate reliably. Moreover, using a single shared hyperparameter configuration across diverse Atari games conflates environment-specific hyperparameter sensitivity with mask/initialization effects: a winning-ticket advantage observed under one hyperparameter choice may disappear (or reverse) under other sensible settings, so the presented averages over three runs do not fully establish robustness across seeds or hyperparameter choices.

nodes.title: RL results use few pruning seeds and shared Atari hyperparameters

nodes.content: The claim that iterative magnitude pruning is the dominant modification for discovering winning tickets is supported in the paper by ablation plots that compare iterative pruning to one-shot pruning and compare late rewinding at a chosen rewind point to resetting to iteration j = 0, but the experiments do not present a systematic sweep over the iterative-pruning rate p, the number of pruning iterations in the NLP experiments, or a range of rewinding epochs that would bound the sensitivity of the dominance claim to those hyperparameters. Fig. 6, Fig. 7

metadata.failure_mode: If alternate pruning rates (smaller/larger p) or different rewinding epochs systematically reverse the relative importance of iterative pruning versus late rewinding in some domains, then the paper's conclusion that iterative pruning is the dominant necessary change must be narrowed: iterative pruning would be an important technique in the reported protocol, but not necessarily the universally dominant mechanism across architectures and hyperparameter regimes. The intermediate link that would fail is the assumption of hyperparameter-insensitivity of the ablation results.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper fixes iterative-pruning rate (p=0.2) and generally uses rewinding to epoch 1 without exploring other p values or rewind points; dominance of iterative pruning may depend on these choices and on interactions with task/architecture. Without a parameter sweep or more fine-grained grid over these hyperparameters, the statement that iterative pruning is the broadly dominant modification across domains is plausible but not tightly established.

nodes.title: Iterative-pruning dominance claim lacks systematic sweep of pruning rate and rewinding epoch

nodes.content: The paper's comparisons use parameter-matched random-ticket baselines that are obtained by drawing new random initial weights and applying the same sparsity mask discovered by iterative pruning, and these random baselines are trained under the same optimization algorithm and the same hyperparameter settings as the winning-ticket retrainings without any per-mask hyperparameter adaptation or additional tuning for masked networks, creating a potential fairness concern insofar as the optimal hyperparameters for training a given fixed mask may differ from those used for the winning-ticket retrainings. Fig. 1

metadata.failure_mode: If random-ticket baselines trained with masks receive mask-specific hyperparameter tuning or optimizers better suited to sparse networks and thereby close the performance gap to winning tickets, then the conclusions that winning-ticket initializations outperform parameter-matched random tickets across pruning levels would be weakened: the superiority would be smaller or vanish in some settings. Mechanistically, the comparative gap would shrink because part of the originally observed advantage was due to baseline under-tuning rather than initialization structure.
metadata.weakness_reason: Parameter-matched random networks can be particularly sensitive to optimizer settings and schedules when trained in sparsified form; if the random-ticket baselines are not tuned to the sparsity-induced training dynamics (for example, different effective learning rates per active-parameter count or different regularization needs), then part of the observed winning-ticket advantage could reflect suboptimal baseline training rather than a genuine initialization advantage. The paper does not report per-mask tuning for random tickets, leaving open a comparative fairness question.

nodes.title: Random-ticket baselines trained without per-mask hyperparameter tuning

nodes.content: For the Wikitext-2 two-layer LSTM configuration (hidden size 650, embeddings 650, truncated BPTT 50, Adam lr=1e-3), the paper reports explicit ablation comparisons (Figure 1) that (a) compare iterative global magnitude pruning (p=0.2) with one-shot pruning, and (b) compare late rewinding to epoch-1 versus resetting to initialization; these ablations show iterative pruning is essential and that late rewinding has a smaller, intermediate effect on language-model perplexity.

metadata.credit: By running controlled ablations within the same LSTM setup the paper isolates the specific contribution of iterative pruning and rewinding to the reported winning-ticket advantage, directly preempting the alternative explanation that the observed effect is a generic artifact of pruning (one-shot) or resetting to j=0; this materially raises credibility that the initialization (not only the pruning procedure) matters in the LSTM experiment and bounds the layer of credibility to the reported LSTM protocol.

nodes.title: LSTM experiments include ablation vs one-shot pruning and rewinding

nodes.content: In Transformer Base experiments on WMT'14 En→De (reported baseline BLEU 27.6), the paper runs a targeted experimental condition that prunes only transformer-layer weights (attention and feed-forward layers) while keeping embeddings intact, and contrasts this with global pruning (all weights pruned) to reveal differing degradation patterns for random and winning tickets (Figure 2 right).

metadata.credit: This targeted pruning ablation isolates the role of embeddings versus transformer layers and provides direct empirical evidence that the two parameter classes respond differently under pruning and initialization; it therefore strengthens the conclusion that the observed embedding/transformer-layer distinction is not purely a byproduct of aggregate reporting but reflects a measurable difference under the paper's pruning protocol.

nodes.title: Transformer experiments isolate transformer-layer-only pruning vs full pruning

nodes.content: The paper trains a Transformer Big model of approximately 210 million parameters on WMT'14 En→De and reports that a model pruned to 67% sparsity and retrained from the winning-ticket initialization achieved BLEU 28.9 compared to an unpruned BLEU of 29.2 (Figure 3), demonstrating sparsification at large model scale.

metadata.credit: The direct demonstration on a state-of-the-art-scale Transformer (210M parameters) is a substantive, load-bearing computational strength: it makes the conclusion about practical compressibility credible beyond toy or small models by showing the effect persists at realistic production scales and thereby supports claims about deployability and practical impact, subject to the caveat about inference runtime support.

nodes.title: Large-scale Transformer Big demonstration at 210M parameters

nodes.content: For the three classic-control environments (CartPole-v0, Acrobot-v1, LunarLander-v2) the paper trained FC networks using A2C and reports mean ± standard deviation across three independent iterative-pruning runs per game along with reward curves showing winning tickets outperform random tickets (Figure 4).

metadata.credit: Although the seed count is modest, reporting mean±std across independent iterative-pruning runs and plotting the resulting reward curves provides direct evidence that the winning-ticket advantage in simple RL control tasks is not a single-run fluke and guards against the simplest kind of over-interpretation based on one run; this underwrites the qualitative claim that winning tickets can be found in classic-control RL settings.

nodes.title: Classic-control RL experiments report mean±std across three pruning runs and show consistent winning-ticket advantage

nodes.content: The paper evaluates nine Atari games with a common convolutional network and shared hyperparameters, reports per-game reward curves (Figure 5) and shading for mean±std across runs, and documents heterogeneous outcomes including several games with clear winning-ticket gains (Assault, Seaquest, Berzerk, Qbert), games that degrade quickly under pruning (Breakout, Centipede), and one case (Kangaroo) where the shared-hyperparameter unpruned model failed to learn but winning-ticket initialization enabled nonzero learning.

metadata.credit: The breadth of the Atari suite and the explicit reporting of heterogeneous per-game outcomes is a substantive strength: it prevents an over-general claim ("winning tickets always help in pixel control RL") and instead supports the more nuanced conclusion about game-dependent utility, while the Kangaroo case supplies direct mechanistic evidence that certain initializations can enable learning in otherwise unstable training settings.

nodes.title: Atari suite evaluation exposes heterogeneous, game-dependent outcomes and a case where winning tickets enable learning where unpruned model failed

nodes.content: The paper presents ablation experiments across representative NLP and RL tasks (Figures 1, 2, 6, 7) that compare iterative magnitude pruning to one-shot pruning and compare late rewinding (epoch 1 or 1000 updates) to resetting to initialization; these ablations consistently show that removing iterative pruning substantially reduces retraining performance while removing late rewinding produces a smaller but measurable effect.

metadata.credit: These cross-task ablations materially support the paper's procedural claim (Conclusion 6) by directly demonstrating that iterative pruning is the more consequential modification across multiple settings; this guards against attributing the observed winning-ticket benefits to unrelated implementation details and increases confidence that the recommendation (use iterative pruning) is evidence-backed within the explored regimes.

nodes.title: Ablation across NLP and RL shows iterative pruning more impactful than late rewinding

steps.reasoning: Start from the upstream result established earlier: iterative magnitude pruning with $p=0.2$ and late rewinding to epoch $j=1$ materially improves the ability to find winning tickets across domains, i.e., treat the conclusion that iterative pruning is crucial and late rewinding is helpful as given.

Specify the two-layer LSTM language-model architecture and training hyperparameters used to test whether winning tickets exist in recurrent models: define Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) as the gated recurrent unit used; hidden state size $=650$; word embedding size $=650$; dropout layer between the two RNN layers with dropout probability $=0.5$; truncated Backpropagation Through Time (truncated BPTT) sequence length $=50$; training batch size $=30$; optimization algorithm Adam (an adaptive stochastic-gradient optimizer) with learning rate $10^{-3}$ and hyperparameters $\beta_1=0.9, \beta_2=0.999, \epsilon=10^{-3}$.

Define the pruning and rewinding procedure applied to the LSTM experiments: global magnitude pruning is applied (i.e., magnitudes of all weights and biases pooled across layers and the smallest magnitudes pruned first), iterative pruning is performed with iterative pruning rate $p=0.2$, and late rewinding is applied by resetting surviving weights to their values after the first epoch of training (i.e., $j=1$ epoch).

Define ticket evaluation for language modeling: after pruning and rewinding, the pruned sub-network (the candidate "winning ticket") is retrained for 10 epochs on the training set, and final performance is measured as the test-set log perplexity (define "log perplexity" as the natural logarithm of the perplexity metric used to assess language-model quality in the paper's experiments).

Report the empirical result from the LSTM experiments: winning-ticket initializations found via iterative global magnitude pruning ($p=0.2$) with late rewinding to epoch 1 produce sparse sub-networks whose retrained performance achieves lower test-set log perplexity than parameter-matched randomly initialized sparse networks for all tested pruning fractions; the authors explicitly state that winning tickets retain high performance even when up to $90\%$ of parameters are removed, and at extreme pruning levels winning tickets show little to no increase in log perplexity compared to the unpruned model while randomly initialized tickets degrade substantially.
Fig. 1

Report the ablation evidence specific to LSTMs that supports the role of iterative pruning and late rewinding: when late rewinding is removed the performance is only slightly damaged (primarily at intermediate pruning levels), while when iterative pruning is removed (i.e., using one-shot pruning) performance plummets and reaches values worse than random tickets once $80\%$ of parameters have been pruned—this establishes iterative pruning as essential and late rewinding as helpful but not strictly necessary for LSTM language modeling.
Fig. 1

Conclude for this domain: therefore, for the two-layer LSTM language model trained on Wikitext-2 with the specified architecture and optimizer settings, iterative global magnitude pruning with $p=0.2$ plus late rewinding to epoch 1 produces winning-ticket initializations that outperform parameter-matched random sparse networks across pruning levels, and winning tickets retain high performance up to $90\%$ parameter removal.

Start from the upstream result established earlier: iterative magnitude pruning with $p=0.2$ and late rewinding to epoch 1 materially improves the ability to find winning tickets across domains; treat that as given for deriving the Transformer conclusions.

Specify the Transformer experimental setup and evaluation metrics: define "Transformer Base" as the Transformer variant trained following the described recipe, trained for $50{,}000$ updates with checkpoint averaging; evaluation uses case-sensitive tokenized BLEU (bilingual evaluation understudy) computed with the provided multi-bleu.pl script on the Newstest2014 test set; the authors report a baseline BLEU of $27.6$ for Transformer Base on Newstest2014.
Fig. 2

Define the pruning and rewinding procedure for Transformers: apply global iterative magnitude pruning with iterative pruning rate $p=0.2$ and apply late rewinding by resetting surviving weights to their values after $1000$ parameter updates (i.e., the authors compare rewinding to the parameters after $1000$ updates), then retrain the pruned network from the rewound initialization and measure BLEU at convergence.

Report the first empirical observation for Transformer Base: winning tickets produced by global iterative magnitude pruning with late rewinding outperform parameter-matched random tickets in BLEU across pruning fractions, i.e., the pruned-and-rewound networks trained from winning-ticket initializations retain higher BLEU than randomly initialized sparse networks at the same sparsity levels.
Fig. 2

Report the empirical observation comparing pruning of Transformer-layer weights versus embeddings: when only Transformer layer weights (attention and fully-connected layers) are pruned while embedding matrices are left intact, random-ticket performance degrades rapidly as pruning increases, whereas winning-ticket performance remains robust and exhibits an approximately linear decline in BLEU as pruning increases—this behavior indicates embeddings react differently to pruning than Transformer-layer weights, and winning tickets principally preserve Transformer-layer performance under this pruning regime.
Fig. 2

Report the ablative insight specific to Transformers and attribute the procedural cause: the authors find iterative pruning and late rewinding significantly improve Transformer pruning outcomes and note iterative pruning has a larger effect than late rewinding; the authors argue that prior work reporting negative findings for Transformers used one-shot pruning and no late rewinding, which can explain the discrepancy.
Gale et al. (2019)

Conclude for this domain: therefore, for Transformer models trained on WMT'14 English→German, global iterative magnitude pruning with late rewinding yields winning-ticket initializations that outperform parameter-matched random tickets, and pruning Transformer layers while leaving embeddings unpruned reveals distinct behavior between embeddings and Transformer-layer weights.

Start from the upstream result established earlier: iterative magnitude pruning with $p=0.2$ and late rewinding to early-training weights materially improves the discovery of winning tickets; treat that as a known procedural foundation for the Transformer Big experiment.

Describe the Transformer Big experimental configuration: define "Transformer Big" as the larger Transformer variant used by the authors with approximately $210$ million parameters; the unpruned Transformer Big model achieves a BLEU reported by the authors around $29.2$--$29.3$ on Newstest2014 (the paper states $29.3$ in the body and compares to earlier work), and the authors apply global iterative magnitude pruning with late rewinding and retrain pruned networks from their rewound initializations.
Fig. 3

Specify the pruning target and measurement: the authors prune to $67\%$ sparsity (i.e., $67\%$ of the parameters removed, retaining $33\%$ of parameters), then retrain the resulting pruned network from the winning-ticket initialization and measure BLEU at convergence; the authors report the retrained pruned model achieves BLEU $=28.9$ at $67\%$ sparsity.
Fig. 3

Compare pruned vs. unpruned BLEU and report the authors' interpretation: the authors compare the pruned-model BLEU of $28.9$ at $67\%$ sparsity to the unpruned BLEU reported as approximately $29.2$ (or $29.3$ as stated elsewhere) and state that $28.9$ corresponds to about $99\%$ of the unpruned model's BLEU; this is presented by the authors as demonstrating that Transformer Big can be pruned to one-third of parameters while retaining roughly $99\%$ of original BLEU when using iterative pruning and late rewinding.
Fig. 3

Conclude for this domain-scale experiment: therefore, with global iterative magnitude pruning and late rewinding the authors demonstrate a Transformer Big model (≈210M parameters) can be pruned to $67\%$ sparsity (retaining $33\%$ of parameters) and, when retrained from the winning-ticket initialization, achieve BLEU $=28.9$, which the authors report is approximately $99\%$ of the unpruned model's BLEU.

Start from the upstream result established earlier: iterative magnitude pruning with $p=0.2$ and late rewinding to epoch 1 materially improves winning-ticket discovery across domains; treat iterative pruning plus late rewinding as the pruning/resetting method used for RL classic-control experiments.

Describe the classic control experimental setup and network specifications: define the classic control environments evaluated as CartPole-v0, Acrobot-v1, and LunarLander-v2; specify the network architectures from the appendix Table A1 as multi-layer perceptrons (MLP) with layer sizes: CartPole MLP(128-128-128-out), Acrobot MLP(256-256-256-out), LunarLander MLP(256-256-256-out); define A2C as the synchronous Advantage Actor-Critic algorithm used to train policies and value functions; for classic control optimization, RMSprop optimizer with learning rate $10^{-4}$ and hyperparameters $\alpha=0.99, \epsilon=10^{-8}$ is used.
Fig. 4
Fig. 6
Table A1

Define the RL ticket evaluation metric: for each ticket, train the ticket for $N$ epochs (where an epoch corresponds to $M$ game episodes or batches as defined per environment), then compute the averaged episodic reward over the final $L$ episodes as the ticket reward; report mean $\pm$ standard deviation over three independent iterative-pruning runs to measure variability.
Fig. 4
Table A1

Report the empirical result for classic control: iterative global magnitude pruning with late rewinding yields winning-ticket initializations that, after retraining from the rewound initialization, produce higher average episodic reward over the final evaluation episodes than parameter-matched randomly initialized sparse networks across pruning levels; this winning-ticket advantage is observed consistently across the three independent iterative-pruning runs per game (the authors plot mean $\pm$ standard deviation).
Fig. 4

Report the ablation evidence in classic control supporting the procedural conclusion: ablation studies (varying the use of late rewinding and iterative pruning while holding other training parameters fixed) show that both late rewinding and iterative pruning improve winning-ticket performance in classic control games, with iterative pruning producing the larger effect in many cases—supporting the claim that iterative pruning materially aids winning-ticket discovery in RL.
Fig. 6

Conclude for classic control RL: therefore, in discrete-action classic control environments trained with A2C and the specified fully-connected networks, iterative global magnitude pruning with late rewinding produces winning-ticket initializations that, upon retraining, yield higher final averaged episodic rewards than parameter-matched random sparse networks across pruning fractions.

Start from the upstream result established earlier: iterative magnitude pruning with $p=0.2$ and late rewinding to epoch 1 materially improves winning-ticket discovery across domains; treat that as the pruning/resetting basis for the Atari experiments.

Describe the Atari experimental setup: define the Atari suite as nine pixel-control games (Assault, Berzerk, Breakout, Centipede, Kangaroo, Krull, Qbert, Seaquest, Space Invaders) trained with a common convolutional network architecture summarized in Table A1 (four convolutional layers with filter sizes and channels specified, followed by MLP(1920-512-512-out)); define A2C as the Advantage Actor-Critic algorithm with importance-factor correction used for training; for pixel-control optimization the authors use Adam with learning rate $10^{-3}$ and $\beta_1=0.9, \beta_2=0.999, \epsilon=10^{-3}$; training uses many parallel game threads (1024) and shared hyperparameters across games.
Table A1

Define ticket evaluation and reporting for Atari: for each pruned ticket, train for $N$ epochs (with $N$ and epoch definitions per Table A1), compute averaged episodic reward over the last $L$ episodes, and plot ticket reward curves for winning tickets (WTs) and random tickets (RTs) as fraction of weights pruned increases; report mean $\pm$ standard deviation across three independent iterative-pruning runs per game as shown in the figures.
Fig. 5

Report the heterogeneous empirical outcomes across games: some games (Assault, Seaquest, Berzerk, Qbert) show substantial average-reward improvements for winning-ticket initializations relative to random tickets; other games (Breakout, Centipede) are highly sensitive to pruning and degrade quickly with pruning; Krull shows little difference between winning and random tickets even at extreme pruning fractions, which the authors interpret as evidence of extreme over-parameterization in that game.
Fig. 5

Report the Kangaroo exception and its significance: the authors used identical hyperparameter settings across all games, and under those shared settings the unpruned Kangaroo models failed to converge to high reward; nonetheless, winning-ticket initializations substantially improved learning compared to random tickets for Kangaroo, enabling nonzero learning where the unpruned models had failed to converge to high reward—this demonstrates cases where winning tickets permit learning that otherwise did not occur under the shared training regimen.
Fig. 5

Report additional observed variability in pruning curves: the authors note that the shape of pruning curves for random tickets varies by game—for example, Breakout and Space Invaders are extremely sensitive to pruning with immediate performance drops, whereas Berzerk, Centipede, and Krull sometimes see performance increases in early pruning iterations—this supports the view that effective over-parameterization and sensitivity to sparsification are highly game-dependent.
Fig. 5

Report ablation results specific to Atari: in ablation studies across representative pixel-control games the authors observe that both late rewinding and iterative pruning tend to improve winning-ticket performance, although the magnitude of improvement varies substantially across games, indicating that the relative importance of rewinding and iterative pruning can be game-dependent.
Fig. 7

Conclude for Atari: therefore, iterative magnitude pruning with late rewinding produces heterogeneous winning-ticket benefits across Atari games—some games exhibit large gains from winning-ticket initializations, some show little or no benefit, and in some cases (e.g., Kangaroo) winning tickets enable learning where the unpruned training regimen did not converge—demonstrating that winning-ticket benefits in pixel-control RL are game-dependent.

Define "iterative pruning" as the process in which alternating cycles of training and pruning are performed, with a fixed iterative pruning rate denoted $p$ (the fraction of the remaining weights removed at each pruning iteration), and define the fraction of weights pruned after $k$ iterations as $r_k = 1 - (1-p)^k$, where $k$ is the pruning iteration index and $1 \leq k \leq 20$; the authors use an iterative pruning rate $p = 0.2$ in their experiments and perform up to 20 pruning iterations in RL experiments.
Frankle & Carbin (2019); Han et al. (2015)

Define "late rewinding" as resetting the surviving (unpruned) weights of a pruned sub-network to their values at an iteration $j$ in training (with the original lottery-ticket resetting corresponding to $j=0$); unless otherwise noted the authors set $j$ equal to one epoch (i.e., they reset to the weights after the first epoch of training) for the NLP and RL experiments reported.

State the experimental protocol common to the cross-domain comparison: pruning is performed globally across all parameters (including biases) by magnitude, the authors compare iterative global magnitude pruning (with $p=0.2$) and late rewinding against one-shot pruning and against resetting to initialization ($j=0$), and they evaluate ticket performance by retraining the pruned sub-network from its rewound initialization and measuring final task performance (e.g., test-set log perplexity for language modeling, BLEU for machine translation, averaged episodic reward for RL).

Report the empirical observation in recurrent language modeling (two-layer LSTMs on Wikitext-2): iterative pruning plus late rewinding yields pruned initializations ("winning tickets") that outperform parameter-matched random sparse networks at all tested pruning fractions; ablations show that removing iterative pruning substantially degrades retraining performance, while removing late rewinding causes a smaller but measurable loss—therefore iterative pruning is the dominant required modification and late rewinding is helpful but less critical in this setting.
Fig. 1

Report the empirical observation in Transformer machine translation: iterative pruning and late rewinding produce winning-ticket initializations that outperform parameter-matched random tickets; ablation studies show that iterative pruning again has a larger impact than late rewinding on recovering pruned-model performance, explaining why prior negative reports that used one-shot pruning and no late rewinding found weaker lottery-ticket effects.
Fig. 2
Gale et al. (2019)

Report the empirical observation in large Transformer Big models: iterative pruning with late rewinding enabled pruned Transformer Big models to be trained from winning-ticket initializations to near-unpruned performance (the authors report achieving $28.9$ BLEU at $67\%$ sparsity, i.e., retaining $33\%$ of parameters, which the authors describe as approximately $99\%$ of the unpruned model's BLEU); this again relied on iterative pruning and late rewinding rather than one-shot pruning.
Fig. 3

Report the empirical observation in reinforcement learning: across classic control tasks (CartPole-v0, Acrobot-v1, LunarLander-v2) and Atari pixel-control games, both iterative pruning and late rewinding improve winning-ticket performance relative to one-shot pruning and to resetting to initialization; ablation plots on representative games (classic control and Atari) show that removing iterative pruning substantially degrades sparse-model retraining performance while removing late rewinding has a smaller but still measurable effect in some games—again indicating iterative pruning is the dominant factor for reliable winning-ticket discovery in RL.
Fig. 4
Fig. 6
Fig. 7

Synthesize these domain-specific observations into a cross-domain conclusion: because iterative pruning (with $p=0.2$) and late rewinding (to epoch $j=1$) consistently improve the ability to find winning-ticket initializations and because ablations show iterative pruning has the larger effect in LSTMs, Transformers, classic control, and Atari, the authors conclude that iterative magnitude pruning materially improves winning-ticket discovery across NLP and RL, with late rewinding providing a smaller but still useful improvement depending on the task.

open_questions.content: The authors acknowledge several unresolved scientific issues and practical limitations. First, the advantage of winning-ticket initializations in RL is highly variable across environments: some Atari games show clear gains, others little or none, and the cause of this heterogeneity (e.g., differences in effective over-parameterization, optimization landscape, or sensitivity to shared hyperparameters) remains unresolved. Second, the precise dependence of winning-ticket discovery on pruning schedules, rewinding epoch choice, and other optimizer/hyperparameter settings across architectures has not been fully characterized; optimal iterative pruning rates and rewinding points for different domains are not established. Third, although Transformer Big can be trained from a pruned initialization to within $1\%$ BLEU of the unpruned model at $67\%$ sparsity, practical deployment would require efficient sparse-matrix libraries and inference runtimes to realize computational and memory gains—such systems are outside the scope of this work. Fourth, the experiments show high run-to-run variance in some RL settings and a need for multiple pruning seeds; understanding and reducing this variance, and determining whether winning tickets generalize across random seeds or across related tasks (transferability of masks/initializations) remains open. Finally, the work does not resolve whether structured pruning methods or alternative ranking criteria could yield better or more transferable winning tickets in NLP and RL, nor whether lottery-ticket phenomena extend uniformly to other large-scale tasks, training regimes, or architectures not evaluated here.
